newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hongkong Telecom deal disappointing, analysts say.
newsitem.headline: Hongkong Telecom deal disappointing, analysts say.

text.p: After months of speculation that Hongkong Telecom would woo a new and influential Chinese partner, investors were left cold on Friday when it merely swapped one passive shareholder for another, analysts said.
"This certainly is just an anticlimactic development," said Andrew Fernow, director of research at Vickers Ballas. "It was simply the transfer from one passive shareholder to another."

Hong Kong-based conglomerate CITIC Pacific Ltd said on Friday it had agreed to sell its 904.69 million shares, or 7.74 percent stake, in Hong Kong Telecommunications Ltd to China Everbright Holdings Co Ltd.

China Everbright, an unexpected partner, is a holding company controlled by China's State Council. CITIC Pacific's parent, China International Trust & Investment Corp, is also controlled by the State Council.
China Everbright and China International Trust & Investment both have an equal stake in China's second telephone network China United Telecommunications Corp (Unicom).

"I don't think that there is a lot of difference between CITIC and China Everbright. My personal feeling is that CITIC is a bit more influential and certainly more high profile," said Jeff Camp, vice president at Morgan Stanley.
"There is nothing more strategically that China Everbright brings to the table," he added.
The deal has left analysts waiting for more.

CITIC Pacific had been expected to sell its stake in Hongkong Telecom after it cut its holding to eight percent from 10 percent in June last year and said it had decided to refocus its investment strategy.

But analysts had also expected Cable & Wireless Plc, which holds 58.5 percent of Hongkong Telecom, to be involved in a deal which could have possibly brought in China's powerful Ministry of Post and Telecommunications (MPT).
"If the market was waiting for a Cable & Wireless deal, this was not it. This could be a step to further evolution," said one analyst, who asked not to be named.
"This was more of just a shifting in shareholding."

Analysts said Hongkong Telecom was still likely to be looking for a strategic partner in China, where regulations restrict foreign companies from direct participation in the telecommunications market.
"They have not moved aggressively into China for the simple reason that the restriction on foreign ownership has remained in place and they don't want to try to challenge that," said Fernow.
"At this point they are probably still looking for strategic shareholders and developing relationships accordingly and I am not sure if the Everbright relationship will be fruitful," he added.
"The market won't be positive. It is going to be downplayed as not holding up much potential."
Shares in Hongkong Telecom were furiously bid up this week in anticipation of a deal, rising HK$1.80, or 13.6 percent, before trading was suspended on Friday morning pending the announcement.

"I think the reason originally was anticipation that whoever would buy the shares would have extra value for Hongkong Telecom either in the form of relationships into China or tangible projects, which is clearly not the case in this transaction," said Camp.
"At HK$15.00, Hongkong Telecom is a bit overvalued by about 10 percent," he said.
Investors showed their disappointment in the deal after trading in Hongkong Telecom shares resumed on Friday afternoon.
The stock shot to a high of HK$15.90 before closing at HK$14.50, down HK$0.50.
